case.name: US Debt Crisis and Adjustment (2007-2011)
case.period: 2004-2011 (bubble 2004-2006; top 2007; depression 2008; transition 2009; beautiful deleveraging mid-2009 to 2Q 2011)

source.book: Ray Dalio, Principles for Navigating Big Debt Crises (Bridgewater, 2018), Part 2

phases.template_phase: Early (healthy) part of the cycle / set-up
phases.notes: 1990s debt/GDP rose only a little with strong income growth and low unemployment. 2001 recession (tightening, dot-com bust, 9/11) led the Fed to cut from 6.5% to 1% -- 'note how close the US rate was to 0 percent'. Cuts stimulated household borrowing; set the stage for the bubble.

phases.book_section: The Emerging Bubble: 2004-2006 (The Housing Market Debt Bubble; The Emerging Broader-Based Bubble; shadow banking)
phases.notes: Goldilocks optics (growth 3-4%, unemployment 4-5%, inflation 2-3.5%, GDP gap 2%) while debt/GDP grew 12.6%/yr on average and housing ran a classic 7-signal bubble; Fed raised rates gradually from 1% (2004) to just over 5% (2006) looking at inflation/growth, not debt growth. Leverage migrated to shadow channels (repo/CP, institutional depositors, money funds, global dollar lending, securitization). Home prices peaked April 2006.

phases.dates: 2007 (first half: new highs; summer: credit cracks; fall: contagion while stocks make the Oct 9 high)
phases.book_section: The Top: 2007 (The First Half of 2007; The Summer of 2007; The Fall of 2007)
phases.notes: Tightening to a 5.25% nominal / 1.5% real short rate popped the bubble. Cyclical peak in rates mid-June/mid-July 2007 (10-yr 5.3%, 90-day bill 5%, very flat curve). Bear Stearns funds June; ABX crash July; BNP Paribas Aug 9; Bridgewater's 'This Is the Big One' Aug 10; Fed cut Sept 18; S&P all-time high Oct 9, 2007; write-downs and the Nov 21 Special Report; year ends with S&P -6% from peak but up for 2007.

phases.book_section: Depression: 2008 (Jan-Feb; March Bear Stearns; Post-Rescue Rally Apr-May; Summer Stagflation; Taking Control of Fannie and Freddie; The Crash: September 2008; Lehman Sept 8-15; Aftermath Sept 15-18; Bailout Fund Sept 18-31; October 2008; Nov-Dec 2008)
phases.notes: Bridgewater's own staging inside this phase: 'first stage' (liquidity problems, Fed liquidity works) through early August 2008; 'second stage / avalanche stage' (solvency crisis, forced asset sales) called Aug 18, 2008; post-Lehman described as 'stage 3' (Oct 13 BDO). Policy moved from rate cuts and liquidity (Jan-Mar), to GSE conservatorship (Sept 7), Lehman failure (Sept 15), AIG (Sept 16), TARP (Oct 3), capital injections + FDIC debt guarantees (Oct 13), QE1 (Nov 25), zero rates (mid-Dec).

phases.book_section: Transition from an 'Ugly' to a 'Beautiful' Deleveraging: 2009; Policy Makers Launch Coordinated Counterattack: March-April 2009; The Bank Stress Test
phases.notes: Economy in free fall (500k+ payroll cuts a month). Geithner plan Feb 10, ARRA Feb 17, housing plan Feb 18, TALF, AIG Mar 1; bottom in stocks / top in dollar on March 9; 'shock and awe' QE expansion March 18 (+$1.15tn), PPIP March 23, G20 IMF + FASB April 2; government backstopping ~$29tn (2/3 of all debt) by April; stress-test results May 7 matched Bridgewater's loss estimates.

phases.template_phase: Beautiful deleveraging (reflation: QE + fiscal + macroprudential supports)
phases.book_section: The Beginning of the Beautiful Deleveraging: June-December 2009
phases.notes: Liquidity via QE, capital via fiscal policy and other supports reduced risks and lifted risky-asset prices; inflation fears from 'printing' did not materialize because printing replaced contracting credit. Regulatory wave (June 17 reform proposal -> Dodd-Frank 2010; SEC money-fund rules; CFPA; Reg Z; compensation reviews).

phases.template_phase: Continued reflation / 'sweet spot' recovery; premature tightening scare; QE2
phases.dates: 2010 - mid-2011 (case ends 2Q 2011 when real GDP regained its pre-crisis level)
phases.notes: Markets up ~65% from March 2009 lows entering 2010 and pricing 2-3 Fed hikes; QE1 ended March 2010 ($1.25tn MBS; >$2tn printed in all). Ending QE was itself a tightening; Europe's debt crisis (PIIGS) hit; US stocks fell >15% May-July 2010; yields fell >100bp; Jackson Hole (Aug 27) and QE2 ($600bn, Nov 3). 2010 S&P total return 13%. By 2Q 2011 real GDP back to pre-crisis level with slack remaining (unemployment ~9%, GDP gap ~-3%).

Case study ends: real GDP returns to pre-crisis level; relatively fast recapitalization (TARP repaid), fast unwind of emergency credit programs, good financial returns
timeline.numbers: unemployment ~9%, GDP gap ~-3%, S&P ~1,300 at 2Q 2011 (charts to 2018: unemployment ~4%, S&P ~2,800, gap ~+1%); debt projections: government ~100% of GDP rising to ~110%, households ~75%, financials ~80% falling to ~70%, non-financial business ~70% rising to ~80%

policy.action: Fed cuts funds rate from 6.5% to 1% after the 2001 recession; real short rates negative from late 2001 to early 2006.
policy.assessment_per_author: Made 2001 recession short and shallow but set the stage for the bubble. Classic: central banks accommodate debt growth while watching CPI/growth.

policy.action: Fed raises gradually from 1% (2004) to just over 5% (2006), 15 increases in ~2 years; regulators let shadow banking and securitization grow; concern about competing with London.
policy.assessment_per_author: Not enough to slow debt-financed asset appreciation. The Fed focused on growth/inflation/GDP gap rather than debt growth and whether debts would produce incomes to service them -- the typical mistake behind the worst bubbles (US 1929, Japan 1989). Regulatory system did not keep pace; banks and shadow banks inadequately capitalized and over-leveraged.

policy.action: Paulson confirmed; convenes President's Working Group; pushes GSE reform legislation with Barney Frank (passes House spring/May 2007, stalls in Senate until summer 2008).
policy.assessment_per_author: Relationships among Paulson, Bernanke, Geithner proved critical later. None of the three saw subprime excesses spilling into a nationwide housing decline; the GSE push did not progress until the crisis came to a head.

policy.action: Fed continues tightening to 5.25% nominal / 1.5% real; Bernanke (Mar 28) says subprime impact 'likely to be contained'.
policy.assessment_per_author: The tightening popped the bubble (rates flowed through to ARMs and home prices, which had peaked April 2006). Dalio shared the 'contained' assessment then, though more worried about leverage.

policy.action: ECB injects 95bn euros then 61bn; Fed lends $19bn vs MBS + $19bn reverse repo; BoJ first intervention; Fed cuts discount rate 0.5% between meetings (Aug 17); BofA puts $2bn into Countrywide; banks tap discount window ($500m each at Citi, JPM, BofA, Wachovia).
policy.assessment_per_author: Alleviated most of the funding strains; equities recovered. Bernanke promised more if needed. Coming out of the episode most thought problems contained; Bridgewater disagreed ('day of reckoning pushed forward').

policy.action: Treasury works with lenders/servicers to modify mortgages; Treasury + Fed develop 'break the glass' option to buy illiquid mortgage securities (forerunner of TARP); Bernanke's 'blue-sky thinking' including Section 13(3) lending beyond banks; Fed cuts 0.5% on Sept 18 (vs 0.25% expected).
policy.assessment_per_author: Easing sent the message the Fed would act, but could not solve the fundamental solvency problem (more debt than could be serviced). He endorses erring on providing too much liquidity ('life-blood'); Geithner's view that the moral-hazard framework is wrong in a crisis 'has proven true time and time again'. Geithner's estimate: rescue earned ~2% of GDP instead of losing 5-10%.

policy.action: Banks propose $75-100bn 'super-SIV' fund (Oct 15) -- abandoned Dec 21 as 'not needed at this time'; Paulson teaser-rate freeze measures; Fed cuts 0.25% Dec 11 (less than expected); coordinated central-bank liquidity Dec 12; ECB $500bn (Dec 19).
policy.assessment_per_author: Policy makers were reactive, not proactive; they do not act decisively until the crisis is on top of them. Bridgewater's Nov 21 Special Report ($420bn MTM losses) was shown to Treasury and the White House, who found the picture implausible.

policy.action: Emergency 75bp cut to 3.5% (biggest since Oct 1984) then 50bp more a week later -- largest calendar-month drop in short rates since 1987; Senate passes ~$160bn tax-rebate stimulus.
policy.assessment_per_author: Stocks bounced but by end-February were back where they had been before the Fed acted; credit and economic conditions kept deteriorating. Bridgewater told clients this was a 'D' (deleveraging) not an 'R'.

policy.action: TSLF $200bn (Mar 11); Fed + JPMorgan 28-day secured funding for Bear (Mar 14); Fed $30bn non-recourse loan so JPMorgan buys Bear at $2/share (Sunday Mar 16); new lending facility for 20 investment banks; 75bp cut to 2.25% (Mar 18).
policy.assessment_per_author: Right call: Fed 'did a fabulous job'; failure to act would have passed 'the point of no return'. Key constraint exposed: no legal authority to put capital into a failing investment bank, so a private buyer was required. Rally that followed = a 'currency intervention' that does not change underlying conditions. He also notes Fed could not do it alone -- accounting changes needed and not delivered.

policy.action: Fed cuts 25bp Apr 30 (seventh cut in seven months) and signals pause; TAF raised to $75bn (May 2); Fed holds June 25 citing inflation; Bernanke (June 4) says further cuts unlikely.
policy.assessment_per_author: 'Ugh.' The shift from debt/growth risks to price stability was a mistake in a deleveraging. Using economy-wide interest-rate/liquidity tools for sector debt problems is inefficient; macroprudential tools would have been better and should have been used in 2007.

policy.action: SEC limits shorting of 19 financials (Jul 16); Fed extends PDCF to Jan 30, 2009; Treasury/Fed GSE backstop plan; Congress passes bill (Jul 23; signed Jul 30) giving Treasury 'unspecified' authority (limited only by the debt ceiling) to fund Fannie/Freddie and expanded FHFA oversight; covered-bond initiative.
policy.assessment_per_author: Guarantees of GSE paper were the most unprecedented intervention. Nationalizing too-big-to-fail institutions on the brink is a classic, usually well-received deleveraging move; in own-currency debt the government can eliminate default risk. Paulson's 'unspecified' authority was legal finagling but necessary.

policy.action: Oil falls; relief rally; Treasury examines GSE books -- 'tens of billions underwater'.
policy.assessment_per_author: Underlying credit drivers unchanged; Bridgewater says the second (avalanche) stage is beginning; 'race to the wire'.

policy.action: Fannie and Freddie placed in conservatorship with Treasury guaranteed preferred-stock purchases (no advance warning -- 'ambush'); terms finalized Sept 7, FHFA examiners pressured into agreement Sept 4.
policy.assessment_per_author: Correct and long inevitable; the puzzle is why Treasury waited so long. The NYT's 'turning point' read was wrong.

policy.action: Fed/Treasury convene bank heads; no buyer without government support; Treasury insists none will come; Lehman files Monday Sept 15; Fed expands PDCF to almost any collateral the night before.
policy.assessment_per_author: The policy makers lacked authority to inject equity or guarantee Lehman's book and erred on doing more rather than less within the law -- 'Section 13(3)... did not make them alchemists'. Almost everyone agrees orderly liquidation authority would have been far better: a classic case of political and legal constraints blocking beneficial action. Lehman's interconnectedness ($4-6tn CDS, ~8% of market) made it the 'avalanche'.

policy.action: Fed holds the funds rate (inflation still cited) -- Bernanke later: 'certainly a mistake'; Fed lends AIG $85bn at a floating rate from 11.5% for an 80% stake, collateralized by insurance subsidiaries etc.
policy.assessment_per_author: The AIG loan 'redefined the limits of US central banking' and was courageous but unusually risky; Geithner called it one of his hardest decisions. Bridgewater: the Fed's balance sheet became the safety net, tragically late.

policy.action: SEC tightens short-sale controls; regulators propose accounting relief; TARP concept ($500bn) announced; Fed $180bn new swap lines; SEC bans shorting ~800 financials; Goldman and Morgan Stanley become bank holding companies; Treasury guarantees money-market funds using the $50bn ESF ($45bn legal opinion), limited to funds in trouble as of Sept 19 after FDIC's Bair objected.
policy.assessment_per_author: 'Great Moves!' -- the safety net finally being built; the ESF move was 'exactly the kind of quick thinking and creativity' required. Accounting changes help but do not fix overindebtedness; recapitalization needed.

policy.action: Three-page $700bn TARP proposal (Sept 20); House rejects (Sept 29; S&P -8.8%); FDIC seizes WaMu (Sept 25, JPM pays $1.9bn) and then Wachovia; bill passes Oct 3 with FDIC limit raised $100k -> $250k; later TAG program guaranteeing non-interest transaction accounts.
policy.assessment_per_author: Buying $700bn of mortgages at market prices would not change anyone's condition; at a premium it would be an unethical subsidy. Populist fights over who pays are classic and counterproductive ('doctors in the emergency ward arguing over who will pay'). Political systems act only hours before disaster; shows why regulators need broad emergency authority. Market said the bill was not enough.

policy.action: Fed Commercial Paper Funding Facility under 13(3), buying unsecured CP with no Treasury backstop.
policy.assessment_per_author: Took the Fed to the edge of (or beyond) its statutory authority; 'the Fed bravely did what it needed to do'.

policy.action: G7 commitment (Oct 11); Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program (FDIC guarantees newly issued unsecured bank/BHC debt and non-interest-bearing transaction accounts); Capital Purchase Program -- preferred stock with 5% dividend up to 3% of RWA / $250bn; nine CEOs required to take $125bn (Oct 13); international parallels.
policy.assessment_per_author: The single largest push; TLGP was, per Paulson, the most powerful step (FDIC counsel thought it illegal; Bair backed it). Stocks +11.6% (largest since 1939). Bridgewater: 'doing everything possible' -- would have worked in stage one; in stage three, 'we just have to wait and see'. Putting capital in the banks rather than buying assets was necessary and appropriate; TARP capital came back with ~$50bn profit.

policy.action: Fed expands dollar swap lines; balance sheet more than doubled (+~$1tn); Fed cuts 50bp on Oct 29.
policy.assessment_per_author: Could not relieve the global dollar squeeze (EM worst); dollar +8% in October. Classic.

policy.action: Paulson drops asset purchases; TARP to capital injections for banks and nonbank financials (not autos) plus consumer-lending facility (TALF precursor); Treasury refuses GM's $10bn; Nov 25: Fed/Treasury $800bn -- $600bn purchases of GSE debt/MBS = first QE; $200bn TALF.
policy.assessment_per_author: Shift to capital made sense but rattled markets (S&P -5.2%). QE1 was 'a classic and critical step': central bankers in crises must choose between printing and allowing a big tightening, and they inevitably print. What differed from 1930-33 was the speed. Mortgage rates fell ~1% on the news. Would have been less painful if done earlier.

policy.action: Fed to 0-0.25% ('historic'); $13.4bn emergency loans to Chrysler/GM (Dec 19) via TARP; GMAC becomes a bank; UK $30bn stimulus, EU $258bn plan, China cuts, BoJ unlimited collateralized lending.
policy.assessment_per_author: Zero rates + QE marked the moment things reversed; in both 1930s and 2008 markets and economy bottomed right after money printing began. QE is 'a giant shot of adrenalin'; the only question was whether it had come too late. Auto rescue emblematic of a more forceful approach; the transition between presidents was 'the very best of political behavior'.

policy.action: $20bn more into BofA with up to $98.2bn loss absorption (Jan 16); Geithner Financial Stability Plan with stress tests (Feb 10); ARRA $787bn (Feb 17); $275bn housing plan (Feb 18); TALF up to $1tn (from Mar 5); 'strong presumption' against nationalization (Feb 23); Citi stake to 40%.
policy.assessment_per_author: Markets fell on every announcement (-4.9% on Geithner's speech; -3.5% on the no-nationalization statement) because details were absent; investors expected the worst. Bridgewater thought the stimulus offset only ~1/3 of a $1.2tn credit hole and that nationalization was the best but extremely dangerous option.

policy.action: AIG +$30bn and loosened terms (Mar 1); Fed expands QE by $750bn agency MBS + $100bn agency debt + up to $300bn Treasuries, widens TALF collateral, 'exceptionally low... for an extended period' (Mar 18); PPIP $500bn-$1tn with Fed leverage and loss guarantees (Mar 23); regulatory overhaul plans (Mar 24-26).
policy.assessment_per_author: The coordinated 'shock and awe' counterattack: 'much more aggressive than earlier easings', sequenced as mega-announcements that magnified the market impact. March 18 = inevitable, classic D-process step done earlier than typical; Bridgewater expected Fed Treasury purchases of $1.5-2.0tn. S&P +7.1% on PPIP day. The March 9 bottom came when selling exhausted.

policy.action: G20 adds $250bn immediate IMF financing (toward $500bn new capacity vs ~$250bn existing); FASB eases mark-to-market.
policy.assessment_per_author: 'An enormous wave' -- by April the US government was backstopping ~$29tn, two-thirds of all debt. IMF step big; FASB changes little impact on banks' write-offs, some relief for insurers. GM/Chrysler 'cushioned bankruptcy' plan under Rattner/Summers endorsed as sensible.

policy.action: AIG bonus uproar; House passes 90% bonus tax (Mar 19); calls for Geithner's resignation; Obama stands behind him.
policy.assessment_per_author: Populist 'punish the bankers' calls are classic and make necessary actions harder; judging policy makers for imperfection is unfair (Summers: battlefield medicine). A forced resignation would have had large bad consequences.

policy.action: Stress-test results for 19 largest banks released (adverse scenario: -3.3% GDP, 8.9% unemployment, -22% house prices); banks raise ~$56bn within two weeks; 10 banks repay $68.3bn TARP (June 9).
policy.assessment_per_author: 'We Agree!' -- regulators' numbers nearly identical to Bridgewater's; first time in two years he was confident regulators understood the scale. Geithner took the note to Obama.

policy.action: Financial-reform proposal (Jun 17 -> Dodd-Frank, signed Jul 21, 2010); SEC money-fund rules (Jun 24); CFPA bill (Jun 30); Reg Z changes (Jul 23); Fed compensation review of 28 organizations + TARP Special Master rulings (Oct 22); House passes Financial Stability Council/CFPA (Dec 11).
policy.assessment_per_author: Changing laws in ways that would have made the crisis less bad is typical at the end of big debt crises; over ~25 years they are flouted and new leverage forms produce the next crisis.

policy.action: QE1 ends March 2010 after $1.25tn MBS (>$2tn printed in total); fiscal stimulus peaks; Dodd-Frank; Jackson Hole signal (Aug 27); QE2 $600bn (Nov 3); swap lines extended (Dec 21).
policy.assessment_per_author: Slowing/ending QE is a tightening -- flow matters more than stock. Bridgewater argued (Feb 17) the consensus for restraint was premature and (Jul 29) that the Fed should press the monetization 'accelerator'; QE2 'broadly worked': growth resumed after a lull between QE1 and QE2, S&P +13% total return 2010, inflation expectations re-anchored. Europe made the rookie mistakes (austerity, no printing, no protection of systemically important entities).

policy.action: Real GDP back to pre-crisis level in 2Q 2011; TARP capital repaid; emergency programs unwound.
policy.assessment_per_author: Compared with other countries the US had a relatively fast recapitalization, a relatively fast unwind of emergency credit programs, and good overall financial returns on the rescue; still plenty of slack (unemployment ~9%, GDP gap ~-3%) and a self-reinforcing upward cycle under way.

markets_by_phase.behavior: S&P 500 +35% over three years (earnings +32%, ~10%/yr). Home prices +~30% 2004-06, +>80% since 2000 (index ~85% above Jan-2000 by 2006). Total home sales peaked ~8.4-8.5 million annualized in 2005; ~8% of households buying a home a year. Mortgage rates hit 2003 lows (~5.5%, lowest since 1950s) and rose ~1.5% in 2005-07; LTV on new mortgages ~73% (2003) -> 80%; subprime 20% of market. Short rate 1% (2003-04) -> >5% (2006) while long rates stayed ~4.5-5% and the curve went from -3.5% to inverted; real short rates negative late 2001-early 2006. Savings rate ~7.5% -> ~3%. Current account -6% of GDP; portfolio inflows ~10% of GDP. Securitized issuance ~$2.1tn (2006); ABCP ~$1.2tn (2007); repo liabilities of broker-dealers x2.5 in four years. 2005 trade deficit $725.8bn. Corporate spreads ~1% and realized equity vol ~10% in early 2007 -- 'tranquil and priced to stay that way'.

H1: S&P rallies to ~1,550, records in April-May; Dow +337 pts in three days (Mar 22); 10-yr 5.3% mid-June (highest since 2002), 90-day bill 5% mid-July -- the cyclical peak. June: Bear Stearns funds fire-sale $3.6bn. July: ABX AAA 2007 tranches from 9bp to 440bp; new home sales ~16m -> ~8m annualized; financial equity index peak ~120 -> ~103; July ends -6% from peak. Aug 9-10: BNP freeze, TED spread spikes to ~2.4%; S&P from ~1,550 to ~1,410 then recovers to ~1,480 after the Aug 17 discount-rate cut; 10-yr 4.37% (Sept 7). Sept 18: 0.5% cut puts S&P within 2% of all-time high; Oct 9, 2007 all-time high (not regained until 2013). Oct 19: -2.6%. Dec 11: biggest December sell-off on a 0.25% cut. Year-end: S&P -6% from October peak but +5.5% total for 2007 vs Treasuries +8.5% (first outperformance since 2002); 10-yr ~5% (June) -> ~4%; dollar index -8.6%; oil +55% to $96; Bear 3Q07 earnings -61%, Morgan Stanley -7%, Lehman -3%; Citi initial write-down $5.9bn; MBIA -26% (Dec 20).

S&P -~10% by Jan 20; global equities worse; -1.25% one-month drop in short rates (largest since 1987). Rally after Jan 22/30 cuts fully reversed by end-Feb. First 10 days of March -4.5% (financials worse); Bear CDS ~7%, Lehman/MS ~4%; Bear's $18bn cash gone Mar 10-14; stock from $173 peak to $2. Mar 11 TSLF: Dow +416.66 (~4%, largest in 5+ years); Mar 18: Dow +420; March ends flat. Post-rescue (Apr-May): S&P +~8% from rescue level, 10-yr ~3.3% -> ~3.9%, bank CDS from ~2.7% peak to ~1.2%, corporate spreads from ~3.5% to ~2.8%; markets price Apr 30 cut as last. Oil $130 (late May) -> $138 (June 6) -> >$142 (June 27); headline inflation ~5.5% y/y; CPI 4.4% May. June: S&P -9%; Dow -20% from Oct 9, 2007 high (11,327); unemployment 5.6%; consumer confidence 16-yr low (~50); consumer loan delinquency ~2.8% -> ~3.7%, mortgage delinquency ~4.7% -> ~7.0%; real trade-weighted dollar ~-12%. July 7-15: Freddie/Fannie -~45% each in a week, Freddie -23.8% on July 10; GSE equity -75% in under a year; agency 10-yr spreads from ~0 to ~1.8%. July 15 turning point: oil -$17, short-sale limits; S&P +~7% to August; August equities +~2%, financials -1%.

First week: oil to five-month low, Dow -344.65 (Sept 4), unemployment 6.1%, stocks -2.5%. Sept 8: +~2% on GSE takeover. Sept 9: Lehman -~50%, Citi/MS/Merrill -5-10%, market -~3%. Sept 11: Lehman -42%; Sept 12: Lehman -17%, AIG -31%, market +0.4%. Lehman CDS ~9%, Merrill ~5%, MS ~4%. Sept 15: S&P -~5% (to ~1,190), banks/insurers -~10%, financial equity index ~19 -> ~15. Sept 16: Reserve Primary breaks the buck; money-fund assets had grown ~$1.9tn (2005) -> ~$3.5tn. Sept 17: -~4.7%, 3-month bill ~0% (from ~1.6%), Libor ~2x prior week, MS spreads above Lehman's Friday level. Sept 18-19: rally, +4% Friday. Sept 22: -3.8%, dollar down, commodities up. Sept 29: -8.8% (largest since 1987), oil -~$10, bills ~0. AIG share price from ~$1,100 (Sept 2007, as printed) to ~$0.

Oct 1-10: S&P -22% with no up day; Oct 9 -7.6% on record volume; Dow/S&P -18% for the week (worst in >=75 years); oil to $75 mid-month; PMI ~39; weekly claims ~480k; Oct 3 TARP passage -1.4%. Oct 13: S&P +11.6% (largest since 1939), Dow +936. Oct 15: -9%; Oct 16: +4.3%. Oct 20: CP rates at four-week lows, interbank easing; TED spread peaked ~4.6%. Oct 28: S&P +>10%; Oct 29: -1.1% on 50bp cut. October: S&P -17% (largest month since Oct 1987); dollar +8% (dollar squeeze, worst in EM); Fed balance sheet +~$1tn.

Retail sales -8%, auto sales -30% y/y, unemployment >6.8% (highest since 1994), company profits ~-35% y/y, December manufacturing worst since 1982. Nov 12: -5.2% on TARP shift. Nov 19: -6.7% (52% below Oct 2007 peak). Nov 20: new low, >-20% for the month; oil <$50; claims 16-yr high. Nov 21-28: Dow +16.9%, S&P +19.1% in five sessions on Geithner/Summers news and QE1; 30-yr mortgage 6.3% -> 5.5%, 10-yr -22bp; November S&P -7.5%. Implied vol peaked ~65% (Nov 20); 10-yr yield ~2.1% by late December; December: rates to zero, dollar fell, stocks rallied; volatility priced to stay high. Policy rates Dec 08: US ~1.0 -> ~0.1%, euro area ~3.25 -> ~2.5%, Japan ~0.3 -> ~0.1%, UK ~3.0 -> ~2.0%. Bridgewater posted significant gains in 2008.

Jan: 62,000 job cuts in one day; ISM 32.4; S&P from ~88% of Jan-1 level to ~68% by Mar 9 (chart). Feb 10: -3% during Geithner's speech, -4.9% on the day; Feb 23: -3.5%; Feb 25: Dow gives up a 236-pt rally. Q4 GDP -6.2% annualized; -598k (Jan) and -651k (Feb) jobs; AIG $62bn loss. March 9: -1% -- the bottom in US stocks (S&P ~675) and the top in the dollar; Mar 10: +6.4%, Citi +38%. Mar 18: 10-yr yields -48bp (biggest in decades; futures ~121.5 -> ~125), S&P futures ~770 -> ~795, dollar -2% vs euro/yen average, gold ~$890 -> ~$945. Mar 23: S&P +7.1%, financials +18%. Mid-April: S&P +25% from low, oil +>20%, bank CDS -~30% (from ~5.2% peak); earlier bear-market rallies of 11%, 12%, 19% (one week in late Oct 2008), 24% (last six weeks of 2008) had all failed; this one (27% by Apr 10) held. Stress-test week: unemployment 8.9%; banks raised ~$56bn; June 9 ten banks repay $68.3bn.

S&P from ~675 (Mar 9) to ~1,100 (Dec 2009); Dow >9,000 (Jul 23); equity implied vol from ~65% (Nov 20, 2008) to ~22%; aggregate corporate spread from ~7.5% (Dec 9, 2008) and ~6.5% (Feb 20/Mar 13, 2009) to ~2.5%; unemployment 9.4% (May), 9.5% (June); weekly claims 550k (Aug) vs 650k peak; inflation fears from printing did not materialize.

Markets +~65% from March 2009 lows entering 2010; futures priced ~225bp of tightening by mid-2011. Jan 22, 2010: 3-day slide -~5%. Greek 5-yr CDS to ~9% (May 2010), Portugal ~4%. S&P +~10% through late April then -15%+ May-July; bond yields -100bp+ over four months; 10-yr breakeven -50bp to ~1.95% before Jackson Hole, then ~2.6%; PMI ~58 -> ~55 -> ~58; consumer confidence ~80 -> ~74 -> ~84; weekly claims ~460k, unemployment ~9.6% (still near highs). 2010 S&P total return 13%; Dow/S&P highest since 2008 (Feb 1, 2011); Dow >12,000 (Mar 20, 2011). By 2Q 2011 real GDP at pre-crisis level; unemployment ~9%, GDP gap ~-3%, S&P ~1,300 (vs ~2,800 and unemployment ~4% at the 2018 writing).

reads.title: The U.S. Housing Bubble
reads.claim: US housing, frothy for a few years, is now a 'full-blown bubble'; its popping would be worse than an equity fall because the house is the household's largest, most leveraged asset; losing more than one's equity can paralyze the economy.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: home prices peaked April 2006 and the housing bust drove the crisis; household balance sheets became the core problem (p189, p194).

reads.title: How Big A Problem Will the Housing Slowdown Be?
reads.claim: Economy humming except housing; is housing 'the dead canary in the coal mine'? 'We're wrestling with this'.
reads.outcome_per_author: An open question at the time; he notes none of the top policy makers (nor he) saw subprime spilling into a nationwide housing decline until later (p178).

reads.title: Growing Financial Risks
reads.claim: Markets discount the lowest risks in decades while embedded risks are large; money thrown at financial instruments like art and jewelry; carry bid up, volatility shrunk, low vol assumed to persist, leverage used to squeeze returns from 'puny spreads'.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: spreads and volatility blew out from July-August 2007; his VAR critique (p190) explains why leverage had built on low vol.

reads.title: Subprime Mortgage Fallout
reads.claim: Investment banks' structured products (CDOs, CMOs, synthetic CDOs) opened credit to risky borrowers; originators stopped underwriting; 'early payment defaults' (New Century: 2.5% of loans missed first payment) are forcing buybacks lenders cannot fund; several dozen subprime lenders already bust.
reads.outcome_per_author: New Century filed for bankruptcy April 2 (sidebar p183). He admits that, like Bernanke (Mar 28 'contained'), he thought the damage would be contained, though more worried about leverage.

reads.title: Glancing at Implied Vols
reads.claim: Slight pickup in implied vol across markets from the lowest levels in more than 10 years; currency, bond, commodity vol still very low; equity vol closer to normal.
reads.outcome_per_author: Vol then exploded: implied equity vol peaked ~65% in Nov 2008 (chart p234).

reads.title: ABX Crash
reads.claim: Subprime debt market got much worse; price action suggests a player bigger than the Bear Stearns funds is going bust; rout spread to AAA tranches -- 2007 AAA tranches originally paying 9bp of spread now at 440bp.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: American Home Mortgage sought Chapter 11 (Aug 7), BNP Paribas froze funds (Aug 9), markets unraveled in August.

reads.title: Is This the Big One?
reads.claim: Crazy lending and leverage have created a pervasive fragility; rates will rise until the system cracks and greed turns to fear, vol and spreads blow out. 'We had (and now have) no idea exactly when this will occur'; a months-long study of derivatives exposures concluded 'no one has a clue' because exposures can only be seen one level deep; exposures ~4x five years earlier, ~$400 trillion.
reads.outcome_per_author: Within two weeks he declared it the big one (Aug 10). The 'no one has a clue' finding foreshadowed the Lehman contagion problem (p215-216).

reads.title: (untitled -- real economy vs market action)
reads.claim: Statistics still show the real economy 'just fine' heading into the market action, but Bridgewater was 'extremely concerned' the Fed was too sanguine.
reads.outcome_per_author: Fed's Aug 7 statement stayed sanguine; the mortgage market seriously unraveled from Aug 9.

reads.title: This Is the Big One
reads.claim: The unwinding of widely held, irresponsibly created positions has begun -- 'another 1998 or 1994... just bigger'; exact path unknowable because positions are opaque; it will run 'with the speed of a hurricane (over the next four to six months)' and leave weaker credits dead; the game plan (a 'Depression gauge' algorithm based on proximity of rates to zero, debt vulnerability and early deleveraging) governs portfolio and counterparty risk.
reads.outcome_per_author: The dynamic was borne out but took longer: the Fed's Sept 18 cut lifted the S&P to an all-time high on Oct 9, 2007 before the 2008 collapse (p192-193).

reads.title: (untitled -- after the Fed's surprise discount-rate cut)
reads.claim: Unlike most who thought the problems contained, Bridgewater's calculations said the day of reckoning would be pushed forward to a big Fed tightening or a big economic turndown.
reads.outcome_per_author: Consistent with what followed: the problem resurfaced as the economy turned down in early 2008.

reads.title: The Bigger Problem
reads.claim: This is bigger than a 'credit crisis': an extension of too much credit/liquidity, not too little; the household sector has a bad balance sheet and cash-flow outlook, so credit problems will spread even as rates fall and credit stays available, until foreign investors see the US as a bad place to invest.
reads.outcome_per_author: Spreading credit problems borne out through 2008; the dollar fell 8.6% in 2007 (p197) but rallied 8% in Oct 2008 on the dollar squeeze (p228).

reads.title: Falling Home Prices and Wealth
reads.claim: Weaker housing hits via falling construction, housing-related spending, less cash-out borrowing and falling wealth; mortgage-financed spending exceeded 3% of GDP at the peak and will turn negative; construction falling at a 20% annual pace is ~1% drag on real growth; real estate assets peaked at 167% of GDP, so the wealth drop will be ~50% of GDP.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: consumer spending fell 'at an extraordinary rate' in late 2008 (p230).

reads.title: Bridgewater Special Report: What We Think Will Be Contained & What We Think Won't Be Contained
reads.claim: Surfaced subprime/SIV problems will spread but be contained (manageable size, dispersed ownership, plentiful liquidity) given wise coordinated management; latent problems beneath the surface are much larger and more threatening (enormous liquidity, imprudent reach for yield via structured, levered, illiquid investments); nobody including regulators understands the exposures; mark-to-market losses already ~$420bn globally, ~1% of global GDP; unrealized losses much larger than realized, so much larger write-downs are coming.
reads.outcome_per_author: Treasury and White House found the picture implausible. Write-downs followed (Citi $22.2bn, Merrill $14.1bn in Jan; UBS estimated $600bn total in Feb 2008). The 'contained' half proved too optimistic once the latent problems surfaced in 2008.

reads.title: The Really Big Picture; Not Just a Normal Recession
reads.claim: This is a 'D' (deleveraging/depression) not an 'R': an R is a tight-money GDP contraction cured by easing; a D is a financial deleveraging forcing asset sales, equity declines, forced selling, credit contraction and economic contraction in a self-reinforcing cycle.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out per his account: by Nov 2008 the economy was in 'the classic early days of a deleveraging/depression' with monetary policy unable to work normally (p230).

reads.title: Slipping Away
reads.claim: Levered counterparty positions form a 'house of financial cards'; entities failing margin calls (TMA, Carlyle) are stressing dealers; Bear Stearns is in a non-equilibrium state; 'Broker/dealers in our experience cannot survive with financing costs close to Bear's current levels.'
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out within days: Bear's $18bn cash buffer vanished Mar 10-14 and it was sold to JPMorgan on Mar 16.

reads.title: More Liquidity (Good), But No Accounting Change (Bad)
reads.claim: Three things needed to keep the avalanche manageable: liquidity to strained intermediaries, accounting changes so losses can be written off over time, and confidence; the Fed is doing its part, Treasury, Congress and accounting regulators are not.
reads.outcome_per_author: Accounting relief did not come until FASB's April 2, 2009 change; he later blamed the lack of accounting adjustments for the move to a solvency crisis (Aug 18, p211).

reads.title: One can look at today's developments for Bear Stearns...
reads.claim: Today's events are the latest manifestation of the deleveraging process, not isolated news; the investment companies' situation must be understood as such.
reads.outcome_per_author: Bear was rescued/sold that weekend; the broader deleveraging continued as he framed it.

reads.title: We think that the Fed has done a fabulous job...
reads.claim: Fed is doing a great job; moral hazard line drawn where the intermediary's equity is gone but before credit problems pass to others; Fed cannot do it alone (accounting changes needed) and what will be required 'boggles the mind'; 'an avalanche can be prevented, but it can't be reversed.'
reads.outcome_per_author: Markets rallied and ended March flat; but the avalanche came in September once the other actors failed to act in time.

reads.title: (untitled -- on the Bear rescue)
reads.claim: Failure to rescue Bear would have meant the financial system passing 'the point of no return' where blowing-out risk and liquidity premiums become self-reinforcing.
reads.outcome_per_author: He maintains the judgement; the Lehman failure six months later produced exactly that dynamic.

reads.title: The Loan Losses Are Still to Come
reads.claim: Losses so far came from instruments that did not exist in past crises and are largely priced; the losses from 'the old way (bad loans)' are about to come to a head.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: delinquencies climbed through 2008 (p205) and the 2009 stress-test loss numbers matched Bridgewater's (p244).

reads.title: The Real Economy Is Still Weak
reads.claim: Markets have bounced but the real economy is near zero growth and still gaining downside momentum: employment, production, demand and investment all weak and weakening.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: unemployment jumped to 5.6% in June (largest monthly rise in two decades) and stats kept missing (p203, p205).

reads.title: Tracking the Economy's Response to Stimulation
reads.claim: The Fed's stimulation has prevented a total collapse of the financial system but has not improved the real economy.
reads.outcome_per_author: Consistent with the April-May data that came in below expectations (p203).

reads.title: On Wednesday the Fed eased for what is priced in to be the last time in this easing cycle
reads.claim: Markets priced the April 30 cut as the end of easing.
reads.outcome_per_author: The Fed indeed held in June (shifting to inflation) and did not cut again until October (p205, p228).

reads.title: Market Bounces on Bear Rescue
reads.claim: The Bear rescue was like a currency intervention that reverses markets temporarily without changing the underlying conditions.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: the S&P fell 9% in June 2008 as credit problems and stagflation returned (p204).

reads.title: Tough Choices for the Fed lie ahead
reads.claim: Central bankers' headaches come when growth and inflation give diverging signals; market action and Fed rhetoric show growing concern over that divergence.
reads.outcome_per_author: The Fed did pivot to inflation worries in June -- 'Ugh' (p205).

reads.title: Real events are starting to feed back onto financial events
reads.claim: Recent trading reflected a favorable shift in perceptions not grounded in reality; S&P's downgrade of Morgan Stanley, Merrill and Lehman is 'a renewed dose of reality'.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: June S&P -9%, Lehman rumors, Moody's cuts to the bond insurers (p204).

reads.title: Global Shift in Inflation Expectations
reads.claim: Short rates have been hammered as markets wake up to central banks' new emphasis on inflation over growth.
reads.outcome_per_author: Fed held rates June 25 citing inflation (p205).

reads.title: Markets are tightening while the economy is deteriorating and financials are in free-fall
reads.claim: Three months after Bear, conditions are unsustainable: tax rebates propped spending while market prices turned uniformly restrictive; the financial-stock bounce has vanished; market value of leverage is exploding (classic over-leveraged death spiral); bigger losses ahead; not enough healthy banks to absorb the dying ones; sovereign wealth funds have lost their appetite for bank equity; bank asset liquidation will constrain credit.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: GSE collapse in July, Lehman/Merrill/AIG/WaMu/Wachovia in September.

reads.title: All Markets are Trading as One...
reads.claim: All markets trading as one with a July 15 turning point ($17 drop in oil, short-sale limits at record short interest, bank earnings surprises); it cannot last; economic stats through July keep weakening.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: relief lasted through August (equities +~2%) and the crash came in September.

reads.title: Bank Failure Expectations
reads.claim: No disorderly collapse yet because Fed liquidity avoided runs (except IndyMac) and bailouts/buyouts came each time; more failures likely; markets price ~4% of financial institutions going bankrupt within 6 months, implying ~$600bn of asset liquidation, while the banking sector has only about half that in free equity capital, much needed for old-loan losses.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: Lehman, WaMu, Wachovia failed and AIG/GSEs were rescued within three months.

reads.title: Developed World Entering Recession
reads.claim: Growth rates are collapsing at accelerating rates across the developed world; central banks will head toward easing while markets still price tightening.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: coordinated global easing in Oct-Dec 2008 (US and Japan to zero; chart p233).

reads.title: Entering the Second Stage of the Deleveraging
reads.claim: First stage largely done; now entering the second, 'avalanche' stage; Fed provided liquidity but accounting adjustments were not made, so 'we are approaching a solvency crisis... about to result in an avalanche of asset sales'; whether a safety net gets built in time is 'a race to the wire'.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: September 2008 crash; he labels the Lehman stage 'the avalanche' (p216).

reads.title: The Latest Step Down the Inevitable Path of Dealing With Fannie and Freddie
reads.claim: GSE failure and de facto nationalization under the implied guarantee were long inevitable; what is not obvious is why the Treasury waited so long.
reads.outcome_per_author: Consistent with his account; the NYT's 'possible turning point' read the same day was 'wrong' (p213).

reads.title: (untitled -- counterparty uncertainty before Lehman)
reads.claim: Uncertainty is tremendous: settlement with a vanished counterparty, uncollected mark-to-market gains turning you into a general creditor, 'maybe Merrill is right behind Lehman'; the natural response is to concentrate positions with a few firms that must ration capacity, so liquidity falls, costs and volatility rise and feed back into the economy; 'We are getting very close to crossing this line.'
reads.outcome_per_author: Lehman filed four days later; contagion ran through money funds, CP and interbank markets exactly along these lines (p216-218).

reads.title: Where We Are Now
reads.claim: Losses were known and manageable with sensible policies (Fed liquidity, accounting changes, a Treasury/Congress safety net); by innuendo the Treasury and Fed showed willingness to dive into the unknown without a safety net -- 'now we sit and wait to see if they have some hidden trick up their sleeves'; with rates heading to zero and intermediaries broken, 'the classic monetary tools won't work' and the Japan-1990s / US-1930s dynamic will drive things.
reads.outcome_per_author: AIG rescue came the next day and the safety net was stitched together over the following week (p217-221); the Fed's rate hold the next day was later called a mistake by Bernanke.

reads.title: The Fed's Balance Sheet Is the New Safety Net
reads.claim: After letting the system go over the edge, the safety net is being stitched together with the Fed's balance sheet because nothing else exists; exactly what Bridgewater would do, but tragic that it is late and unclear it will save the day.
reads.outcome_per_author: Stocks fell 4.7% the next day; TARP and the money-fund guarantee followed within days (p218-220).

reads.title: Great Moves!
reads.claim: Treasury, Fed and Congress 'finally agreed to agree to build the safety net!!!!'; central banks added $180bn overnight; regulators moved against short sellers; Morgan Stanley frozen and about to be dealt with, Goldman not far behind.
reads.outcome_per_author: Stocks rose Thursday and +4% Friday; optimism faded over the weekend when the three-page TARP outline appeared (p221).

reads.title: This Newest Move by the Treasury Is Shockingly Disappointing
reads.claim: The TARP proposal is extraordinary in the breadth of authority it gives Treasury and its lack of specifics; it undermines rather than builds confidence.
reads.outcome_per_author: Monday Sept 22: stocks -3.8%, dollar down (p221).

reads.title: What Markets Are Saying
reads.claim: Monday's action was a disaster for US policy makers: stocks and Treasuries fell while the dollar collapsed and commodities surged -- consistent with a loss of faith in the US as reserve currency.
reads.outcome_per_author: The dollar then rallied 8% in October on the dollar squeeze (p228-229); he explained the reversal in 'The Dollar Squeeze'.

reads.title: The Proposed Plan Disappoints
reads.claim: Buying $700bn of mortgages will hardly help: at market prices it changes nobody's financial condition and is a small share of what needs buying; at a premium it is an unethical subsidy and buys even less.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: Treasury itself abandoned asset purchases for capital injections (Oct 13, Nov 12), which he calls necessary and appropriate (p223, p231).

reads.title: The Fed Continues the Fight on the Liquidity Front, But it is Not Enough
reads.claim: 'we are in the avalanche phase of the deleveraging'; the steps being considered in Washington are not nearly adequate to reverse it.
reads.outcome_per_author: House rejected TARP Sept 29 and the S&P fell 8.8%.

reads.title: The Plan Is Pretty Good; Now We Have To See How it Is Employed and Whether It's Too Late
reads.claim: The agreed plan gives the government all that was hoped for to restore liquidity, solvency and confidence, but is not as forceful or timely as hoped.
reads.outcome_per_author: Bill failed in the House the next day; passed Oct 3 but markets judged it insufficient (p224).

reads.title: A Credibility Test
reads.claim: Financing of US consumption and the global system runs on faith; the House failure shined the global spotlight on US decision makers; 'the world's financiers (China, OPEC) will decide whether US policy makers have passed the test'; 'There is still a lot to lose.'
reads.outcome_per_author: Bill passed Oct 3 after frantic negotiation; markets kept falling into October (p223-225).

reads.title: Horrible Market Action
reads.claim: Price action around TARP has been very bad, consistent with the view that TARP will not be a game changer; stocks made new lows after the vote instead of the usual buy-the-rumor/sell-the-fact net gain.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: S&P -22% Oct 1-10 without an up day (p225).

reads.title: Supply and Illiquidity
reads.claim: Rising government supply with tight liquidity: dealers cannot finance inventory, hedge funds cannot borrow, foreigners losing confidence in the dollar, and the desire for cash trumps all risk, even the yield-curve risk of a Treasury bond.
reads.outcome_per_author: 3-month bill rates sat near zero and interbank/CP markets stayed frozen until Oct 20 (p223, p228).

reads.title: The Governments Are Doing Everything Possible; Now We Will Have to See If It's In Time
reads.claim: Great moves -- everything Bridgewater had hoped for; would have worked in stage one (i.e., instead of letting Lehman fail) but the crisis is now stage 3; many dominoes are falling beyond government reach and 'we are sure that we don't know of many others'; still, for the first time one can say with confidence the major governments are doing all in their power.
reads.outcome_per_author: S&P +11.6% that day (largest since 1939) but volatility stayed extreme; October ended -17% (p227-229).

reads.title: The Dollar Squeeze
reads.claim: A debt is a short cash position; because of dollar reserve status and surplus recycling, a lot of dollar debt was built worldwide, so tight dollar liquidity creates a squeeze that hits dollar-indebted EM (commodity exporters) and supports the dollar until debtors default or get liquidity; Bridgewater expects to stay long USD vs euro and EM currencies until then.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: dollar +8% in October; the squeeze was worst in EM (p228).

reads.title: The Fed Continues to Try to Get the Dollars Where They Are Needed
reads.claim: Fed liquidity has more than doubled its balance sheet (assets and liabilities up nearly $1tn) yet has not offset private-sector need; the world's dollar debts require this unprecedented push; much of the global system lies outside the Fed's reach.
reads.outcome_per_author: Consistent with his account of the dollar squeeze and swap-line expansion (p228).

reads.title: A Template for Understanding What's Going On
reads.claim: The world economy is in a deleveraging/depression process that will be painful for many; contrary to popular thinking it is not a severe recession but an entirely different process.
reads.outcome_per_author: Framework he applies throughout; November-December data were worse than the most pessimistic feared (p230).

reads.title: Creating Liquidity but Failing to Create Credit
reads.claim: The Fed has swapped T-bills for illiquid, lower-grade, longer-duration credits, giving key entities liquidity, but cannot restart privately funded credit expansion because lending is uneconomic for squeezed creditors; without credit expansion the deleveraging continues until a global debt restructuring.
reads.outcome_per_author: The Fed moved to outright 'printing' via QE1 on Nov 25 -- the step he calls classic and critical (p231).

reads.title: We Are Thrilled with the Fed's Management and Are Hopeful That There Will Be Excellent Management at the Treasury
reads.claim: The Fed sowed the seeds (fast credit growth under Greenspan then Bernanke) and the Treasury let the deleveraging move beyond the manageable, but once the Fed saw it, it behaved superbly, redefining how central banks should act in depressions by replacing rather than relying on impaired institutions to provide credit.
reads.outcome_per_author: Treasury's Nov 12 TARP reversal rattled markets (-5.2%); Geithner's nomination (Nov 20) and QE1 then turned sentiment (p231-232).

reads.title: Understanding the Changing Plans for the TARP
reads.claim: Paulson's shift from unlevered asset purchases to capital injections and to levered mechanisms outside banks (guaranteeing new securitization vehicles) makes sense.
reads.outcome_per_author: Consistent with his verdict that TARP capital was necessary and later TALF-type programs helped (p223, p236).

reads.title: The Need for Bankruptcies and the Risks of Preventing Them
reads.claim: The basic problem is debt service too large relative to cash flows; restructurings that write down debts are needed and bankruptcy is the usual mechanism; the more and sooner the bankruptcies, the quicker the crisis ends.
reads.outcome_per_author: Policy instead went to guarantees and 'cushioned bankruptcy' (GM/Chrysler, p239); the Fed tried to skip the restructuring phase via printing (Mar 18, 2009 BDO), which he endorsed as it worked.

reads.title: The Balance Sheet Problem
reads.claim: The thaw since the Fed injected equity has not stopped the avalanche of credit-market selling; basic arbitrage financing relationships have broken; the economy will be in free fall until new credit is available at sensible rates, which will not happen while dislocations remain; no willingness to use balance sheet even for arbitrages.
reads.outcome_per_author: QE1 was announced four days later; mortgage rates fell ~1% immediately (p231-232).

reads.title: Why We Expect More Shock & Awe And What It Will Mean
reads.claim: The Fed and incoming Treasury understand the deleveraging/depression dynamic and are doing what Bridgewater would do; expect 'shock and awe' from both; today's moves broaden securities bought and amounts spent to cut spreads and add liquidity; 'they will do whatever it takes that they can get away with'.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: zero rates (Dec), March 18, 2009 $1.15tn expansion, PPIP, TALF, ARRA (p233, p237-238).

reads.title: How So Many Investors Lost Money in 2008 & Lessons for the Future
reads.claim: Most investors lost because: (1) far more beta than alpha; (2) beta concentrated in assets that do badly in bad times (stocks, private equity, real estate, credit) rather than Treasuries; (3) risk and liquidity premiums rose a lot; (4) 'alphas' had systematic pro-cyclical biases -- the average hedge fund ~70% correlated with stocks.
reads.outcome_per_author: Bridgewater closed 2008 with significant gains while most had significant losses (p234).

reads.title: Putting the Stimulus Plan In Perspective
reads.claim: Lack of credit supply and demand will create a hole of ~$1.2tn in the economy; the 2009 government stimulus will offset only about one-third of it.
reads.outcome_per_author: ARRA passed at $787bn total (Feb 17); the economy kept contracting through March and only leveled off after the March policy wave (p236-237, p242).

reads.title: The US Economy Remains in Freefall...
reads.claim: Credit contraction is now hitting employment: revenues fell faster than costs in Q4, so businesses cut labor; payroll reductions over 500,000 a month in Nov-Dec; without credit, firms must generate cash internally, magnifying layoffs.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: -598,000 (Jan) and -651,000 (Feb) jobs; unemployment 8.9% by May (p236-237, p243).

reads.title: There wasn't much of a surprise..
reads.claim: Congressional members and staff concluded the Treasury's plan was in its infancy and far from where they expected.
reads.outcome_per_author: S&P fell 4.9% that day (p235).

reads.title: The Eve of Nationalization?
reads.claim: Nationalization seems the best option but is extremely dangerous; its goal is to recapitalize acceptably while sustaining the system's basic infrastructure.
reads.outcome_per_author: Regulators issued the 'strong presumption' against nationalization (Feb 23; S&P -3.5%) and chose stress tests plus capital instead; by May he agreed with their numbers (p235, p244).

reads.title: The Inevitable and Classic Central Bank Purchases
reads.claim: Today's Fed moves were inevitable, necessary and classic D-process steps; Bridgewater's calculations put eventual Fed Treasury purchases at $1.5-2.0tn; the Fed is doing these things earlier than typical, trying to skip the debt-restructuring phase and go straight to credit creation (TALF, PPIF, forbearance).
reads.outcome_per_author: Fed had printed over $2tn by the end of QE1 (p247); the March 9 low held and the beautiful deleveraging began mid-2009.

reads.title: The G20 Agreement on IMF Funding and Accounting Changes
reads.claim: G20 IMF support and FASB changes relieve the squeeze; the IMF step is big (expect a US commitment ~$100bn, total IMF resource increase $350bn); FASB changes will have little impact on banks' ability to write off losses over time, some relief for insurers.
reads.outcome_per_author: He restates in the text that the accounting changes had relatively little impact (p239).

reads.title: (untitled -- on money printing and stimulus)
reads.claim: 'Like pandemics, D-processes come along very infrequently', so there is little history to draw on, and the antidote had never been administered in this dosage.
reads.outcome_per_author: Observation; the dosage (~$29tn of backstops, >$2tn printed) worked without the feared inflation (p240, p245).

reads.title: We Agree!
reads.claim: The stress-test numbers and Bridgewater's are nearly the same; regulators explained exactly what they did; the main difference is horizon (regulators' two-year losses vs Bridgewater's life-of-asset losses) and a slightly worse Bridgewater scenario; maximum capital need probably at end of two years; first time in two years Bridgewater was confident regulators understood the scale.
reads.outcome_per_author: Geithner took the note to Obama ('a good day for the home team'); banks raised ~$56bn within two weeks; 10 banks repaid $68.3bn by June 9 (p244-245).

reads.title: (untitled -- on reflation and inflation)
reads.claim: Reflations do not necessarily cause inflation because they can simply negate deflations depending on how far they go and where the money goes; 'inflation' is an average of things that behave differently -- during reflations in depressed economies labor and productive assets see little inflation while money-sensitive assets (commodities, gold) rise.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: inflation fears from printing did not materialize (p245).

reads.title: The Fed's Withdrawal from Quantitative Easing
reads.claim: Given weak underlying conditions the Fed will keep rates near 0% longer than discounted; rolling down the yield curve stays attractive.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: no hikes; yields fell >100bp in summer 2010 and QE2 followed (p249).

reads.title: Tightening + Over-indebtedness = High Risk
reads.claim: Monetary and fiscal policies are starting to tighten globally while mature economies are over-indebted; doubt they can pull back as planned without unacceptable consequences; European debtor countries' (PIGS) over-indebtedness is comparable to the worst EM debt problems of the past.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: European crisis erupted (Greek CDS ~9%), US stocks fell >15% May-July, and the Fed resumed easing (p248-249).

reads.title: The Coming Tightening
reads.claim: The consensus that central-bank printing and deficits must be reined in is at best premature and at worst dangerous; sharp-pencil analysis shows the plans imply too much restraint absent a pickup in private credit or a realignment of developed vs EM currencies.
reads.outcome_per_author: Consistent with the 2010 slowdown and QE2; he says the QE 'broadly worked' (p250).

reads.title: Changes and Levels in Economic Activity and in Financial Asset Prices
reads.claim: Confusion about 'how things are going' stems from looking at changes vs levels: those watching changes in asset prices are most optimistic; those watching changes in activity and levels of market values less so; those watching levels of activity and its drivers least optimistic.
reads.outcome_per_author: Observation; he stresses the still-large slack (unemployment near highs) in mid-2010 (p249).

reads.title: The Template and the Slowdown
reads.claim: The key difference between Bridgewater's view and others' is the long-term debt cycle, which transpires over a lifetime so few have experienced it; recessions are understood, deleveragings are not.
reads.outcome_per_author: Framing; the summer 2010 slowdown led to Jackson Hole and QE2 (p249).

reads.title: More Will Likely Be Necessary From the Fed
reads.claim: Monetization is seen as risky but inaction during deleveraging and deflation is riskier; monetization is a spigot, not a light switch -- calibrate by watching reactions; 'it is time for the Fed to put its foot back down on the monetization accelerator.'
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: Bernanke's Aug 27 Jackson Hole signal and QE2 ($600bn) on Nov 3 (p249).

reads.title: Another Step Toward More Quantitative Easing
reads.claim: The Fed will have to push much harder than anyone expects because the planned QE will be less effective per dollar than the last stage; impact depends on who gets the money and what they do with it.
reads.outcome_per_author: QE2 followed; he judges it broadly worked (p250).

reads.title: (untitled -- consumers)
reads.claim: Consumers face slow income growth, lower asset prices and much lower borrowing ability from lower wealth, higher debt and lower incomes, so households have not responded to lower rates by saving less or borrowing more.
reads.outcome_per_author: Dudley's Oct 1 assessment of growth drivers was broadly similar; QE2 followed (p249-250).

reads.title: The Next Shoe to Drop: More QE and Devaluations
reads.claim: Classic sequence: deleveragings come from declining private credit growth and require more central-bank money creation and larger deficits; austerity has never worked when problems were big and is eventually abandoned because the self-reinforcing contraction is too painful; all deleveragings studied led to big waves of money creation, fiscal deficits and currency devaluations against gold, commodities and stocks.
reads.outcome_per_author: Borne out: QE2 Nov 3; US finished 2010 strongly (S&P +13% total return); inflation expectations re-anchored (p250).

reads.title: ECB Policy
reads.claim: With growth decelerating, peripheral debt problems and austerity dragging, the ECB's balance-sheet 'normalizing' is a de facto tightening that seems a mistake; it will worsen conditions (pressuring peripheral credits) and eventually force a reversal (lower rates and probably a lower euro).
reads.outcome_per_author: Within this case's window: Ireland rescue prospect (Nov 18), Portugal stress (Dec 1), Fed swap extension (Dec 21); the ECB reversal is outside the narrated range.

reads.title: Increasing Global Divergences
reads.claim: Dividing the world into debtors/creditors with independent vs linked monetary policies: debtors who cannot print face years of hardship; creditors who cannot stop printing because of linked exchange rates will overheat; pressures intensify over 18 months, producing cracks and seismic shifts in the linkages.
reads.outcome_per_author: Beyond the case's end (2Q 2011); not scored in the text.

reads.title: Transitioning Beyond the 'Sweet Spot'
reads.claim: The US is in a post-contraction growth spurt supported by monetary, fiscal and credit improvement; with slack at home (and in Europe/Japan) and overheating in EM, inflation pressure is limited and mostly imported; 2010/11 looks like the 'sweet spot' of the first two years of a recovery, but it depends on the Fed's printing and fiscal stimulus.
reads.outcome_per_author: Case ends 2Q 2011 with real GDP back at pre-crisis level and the recovery self-reinforcing but slack remaining (p251).

lessons.lesson: The particulars (pooled/securitized mortgages, levered investment banks, OTC derivatives) are new ways of creating leverage outside regulated channels; seen that way the case is classic.
Bubbles emerge when central banks focus on inflation and growth and do not worry enough about debt-financed purchases of investment assets.
Debt bubbles form in one or a couple of markets, hidden beneath averages; only pro forma stress tests of the significant areas reveal them and their knock-on effects.
Because houses are bought with borrowed money, price gains have magnified effects on equity, which pulls in more borrowing, buyers and lenders.
The higher prices went, the more credit standards were lowered -- the opposite of what logic would dictate; classic bubble behavior.

Seven defining characteristics of a bubble: high prices vs traditional measures; prices discount further rapid appreciation; broad bullish sentiment; high-leverage financing; extended forward purchases; new buyers entering; stimulative monetary policy inflating it and tight policy popping it.
In bubbles people lever up to bet on continued price rises just as supply is increasing; nonsensical but typical.
The worst debt bubbles (US 1929, Japan 1989) are not accompanied by goods inflation but by debt-financed asset inflation; central banks err by accommodating debt growth while watching CPI.
High debt growth used to fund consumption rather than investment is a red flag because consumption produces no income to service the debt.

Shadow-banking growth is a common bubble feature: new channels avoid regulation, look safe through packaging and guarantees, and have not been stress-tested by a crisis; these innovations often lead to the crisis.
A regulatory system that lacks visibility into and authority over shadow channels, and worries about competitiveness, lets banks become under-capitalized and over-leveraged.
Three classic asset/liability mismatches: borrow short/lend long; lend to risky borrowers for the spread; borrow in one currency and lend in another.

Rising rates raise debt service, cut spending and incomes; a flattening curve raises the return on cash, pulls money out of long-duration and low-grade assets, and negative wealth effects feed back -- the tightening popped the bubble.
Debt crises are self-reinforcing because losses reduce capital, forcing asset sales or less lending, which lowers prices and produces more losses; mark-to-market and leverage amplify this.

Past volatility and correlations are not reliable forecasts of risk; low volatility and benign VAR encourage leverage (ratios near 100:1); leverage is a better indicator of future volatility than VAR.
Knowing which crisis actions the law permits, and how to get them approved, is a classic challenge in democracies with rigid rules and checks and balances.

How the moral-hazard question is handled is one of the biggest determinants of outcomes; above all keep systemically important parts alive, and err toward providing too much liquidity rather than too little.
Letting everything burn means the government ends up taking all the risk through nationalization at far greater cost (Geithner's view, which he shares).
Easing cannot solve the fundamental problem of institutions holding more debt assets and liabilities than can be serviced.
Short-term wholesale funding is like an uninsured deposit -- the same run dynamic as 1930-33 before FDIC insurance.
The securitization machine was data-mining history rather than sound logic; people levered up betting that something that had never happened would not happen.

Policy makers are reactive rather than proactive; political systems do not act until there is broad consensus on an intolerable problem, so they rarely act decisively until a crisis is on top of them.

A 'D' (deleveraging) is not a severe 'R' (recession): an R is a GDP contraction from tight policy that ends when the central bank eases; a D is a self-reinforcing financial deleveraging that causes the financial crisis and the economic crisis.
Early signs of stress in an institution funded short can turn into a run that causes failure within days -- lenders rationally withdraw.
If the debt is in one's own currency and policy makers have the knowledge and the authority, they can manage these situations with limited spill-over, though some pain is inevitable.

The biggest constraint on Geithner, Paulson and Bernanke was lacking the legal authority to make necessary moves; systems designed for normal stability are poorly suited to crises that require immediate aggressive action.
A private-sector solution (a healthier institution acquiring the failing one) is the best option when authority to inject capital is lacking.

Interest-rate and liquidity policies that affect the whole economy are very inefficient for sector-specific debt problems; macroprudential policies are more appropriate and should have been used in 2007.
Government guarantees, implicit or explicit, make risky assets look safer than they are, encouraging leverage and bad debt growth.
Nationalizing too-big-to-fail institutions on the brink is a classic, usually well-received move; with own-currency debt the government can eliminate default risk.
Rules and checks and balances have advantages but during crises what needs to be done may not be done swiftly enough; 2008 was full of close calls that required getting around the rules.
In investing it is as important to know when not to be confident and not to make a bet as it is to have an opinion -- hindsight makes bottoms look obvious when they were not.
A solvency problem can only be dealt with by providing more equity capital or changing accounting/regulatory rules.
Lehman was especially scary because of large and poorly understood interconnectedness.
Blanket protections are needed because the uncertainty itself makes everyone run from any entity that could go under.
Policy makers are constrained from explaining candidly during a crisis because candor can intensify the panic (Paulson).
Mark-to-market rules force fire-sale losses that strain capital and liquidity; accounting relief helps but hiding losses does not restore confidence either.
Guarantees work better than backstops -- when you say something is guaranteed, it is far more reassuring to investors (Paulson).
Quick thinking and creativity (e.g., using the ESF) are required to navigate regulatory and political minefields.
Policy debate in deleveragings classically takes on populist overtones; arguing over who should bear the costs is counterproductive -- save the patient first, decide who pays later.
Legislatures act only at the edge of the precipice; regulators therefore need broad emergency authorities rather than relying on Congress.
Among the most important aspects of managing a crisis is having wise, knowledgeable decision-makers with authority to do whatever it takes.
Doing the unpopular but right thing (recapitalizing banks) is heroic and underappreciated; the capital programs prevented a catastrophe and returned a profit.
Political systems typically make the right decisions only after heated fighting and just hours before disaster.
Policy makers must sometimes act at or beyond the edge of statutory authority (CPFF); fear of unintended consequences must yield to preventing a meltdown.
Price = spending / quantity sold; in crises prices move for positioning reasons (squeezes, rebalancing) unrelated to fundamentals, so volatility stays extreme.
A debt is a short cash position; when dollar liquidity tightens there is a dollar squeeze that supports the dollar until debtors default or get liquidity.

Central bankers in crises must choose between printing money to replace contracting private credit and allowing a big tightening; they inevitably choose to print, and that is when things change -- the speed of this step is what distinguished 2008 from 1930-33.

Investors lost money in 2008 because they held beta rather than alpha, beta concentrated in assets that do badly in bad times, risk and liquidity premiums rose, and 'alphas' had systematic pro-cyclical biases (hedge funds ~70% correlated with stocks).
Both in the 1930s and 2008 rates hit zero and printing followed; in both cases markets and the economy bottomed right after. QE is like a shot of adrenalin to a patient in cardiac arrest.
Investors in bear markets fall into three groups: those clobbered who cut risk at the bottom; those clobbered who held or added on blind faith; and the few who understood and sold high/bought low.
When market pricing already discounts terrible outcomes and the range of outcomes is enormous, it is prudent not to take much of a bet.
D-processes come along infrequently; the antidote (money printing and stimulus) had never been administered in this dosage.
As economic pain rises, populist calls to punish bankers are the norm and make saving the system harder; judging policy makers in this way is unfair -- it is battlefield medicine (Summers).
Tops are made when the rate of buying is unsustainable (people think prices will rise); bottoms when the rate of selling is unsustainable (most people bearish).
Had things gone worse or longer, the capitalist and democratic system would have been at risk of breaking.

Reflations do not necessarily cause inflation because they can simply negate deflations; 'inflation' is an average of many things that behave differently (labor and productive assets vs commodities/gold).
Tighter laws are typical at the end of big debt crises; over ~25 years the hangover fades, euphoria returns, the laws are flouted and new forms of leverage create the next crisis.
Merely slowing or ending QE is a tightening; the flow of purchases matters more than the stock of money.

Europe followed the same sequence: policy makers did not believe a crisis would come until it did, then made the rookie mistakes of leaning on deflationary levers like austerity, not printing, and not protecting systemically important entities.

All deleveragings are due to declines in private credit growth that require more central-bank money creation and larger deficits; austerity has never worked when the problems were big; every deleveraging studied led to waves of money creation, deficits and devaluations.
The first two years of a recovery from a deleveraging look like a cyclical 'sweet spot' (slack plus low inflation) but depend on printing and fiscal stimulus.
The US rescue stands out for fast recapitalization, fast unwinding of emergency programs, and good financial returns; the crisis ended (real GDP regained) in 2Q 2011 with slack still present.
